title: How Druids Worked
summary: Josh and Chuck explore what is actually known about the ancient Druids of the Celtic world, separating solid evidence from conjecture. They cover Druids as a learned, job-based class (teachers, judges, priests, philosophers); their refusal to write things down and oral transmission; Celtic writing in Greek; the sources Posidonius, Julius Caesar and Pliny the Elder and their propaganda and hearsay problems; archaeological finds such as Lindow Man, the Deal Warrior and a possible "doctor" grave; claims of human sacrifice, the wicker man legend and cannibalism (no evidence); the Roman bans under Augustus, Tiberius and Claudius; Stonehenge being older than the Celts; and modern Neo-Druid groups tracing roots to 17th-century antiquarians and Irish myth. The episode ends with listener mail about hotel bed bug practices.

segments.title: Opening banter and Druid stereotypes
segments.summary: The hosts joke about Led Zeppelin's druidic imagery and the Gandalf-like druid look, then note that little is reliably known about ancient Druids and that much is conjecture.

segments.title: Who the Druids were and why they left no writings
segments.summary: Druids were a learned, job-based class of ancient Celts in Britain and France, acting as teachers, judges, priests and philosophers. They did not write down their knowledge, preferring oral transmission to keep their mystique and power, though the Celts were not illiterate and wrote in Greek.

segments.title: Ancient sources: Posidonius, Caesar and Pliny
segments.summary: Knowledge of the Druids comes second-hand from Greek and Roman writers. Posidonius's works are lost. Julius Caesar wrote propaganda supporting Roman imperialism, and Pliny the Elder, writing about a century later, wrote more fantastical accounts through a Roman lens.

segments.title: Archaeological finds: Lindow Man, Deal Warrior and the doctor grave
segments.summary: The hosts describe Lindow Man, found in a Pete bog with signs of strangulation, a blow to the head and a slashed throat, and speculate about ritual sacrifice. They also describe the Deal Warrior, buried with weapons and a crown, and a British grave with divining tools and surgical instruments nicknamed 'the doctor', which some call a Druid burial.

segments.title: Roman bans on Druidism and the Celtic resistance
segments.summary: Roman emperors Augustus, Tiberius and Claudius banned Druidism for Roman citizens and then across the empire under penalty of death, citing claims of human sacrifice. The religion went underground, and the Druids were suspected of fomenting rebellion. A Druid prophecy of Rome burning is mentioned.

segments.title: Human sacrifice, wicker man legend and cannibalism
segments.summary: The hosts discuss whether Druids practiced human sacrifice, which may have happened on a small scale, with legends of wicker man burnings and divination from death throes. They say there is no evidence for cannibalism. They also note the 1973 film The Wicker Man.

segments.title: Stonehenge and Celtic trade and civilization
segments.summary: Stonehenge was built long before the Celts and Druids, so its purpose is unknown, though Druids may have used it for ceremonies around the summer solstice. The Celts had extensive trade routes and an established culture before Rome arrived.

segments.title: Neo-Druids, Irish myth and pop culture
segments.summary: Modern Neo-Druid groups trace their roots to 17th-century antiquarians interested in ancient Irish myth, which may preserve Celtic traditions because Rome never conquered Ireland. Folk horror films and other pop culture have shaped popular images of Druids.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: The hosts wrap up the Druids topic and promote the show's social links and contact information.
